title: Imports and Module Documentation
content: Imports for Euclidean geometry (EuclideanSpace, inner product), finite sets (Finset), real analysis (NNReal, logarithm), and filter convergence. The module formalizes Erdős Problem #100 on point sets with restricted distances in the plane.
mathContext: The formalization works in $\mathbb{R}^2$ modeled as `EuclideanSpace \mathbb{R} (Fin 2)` with the standard inner product inducing the Euclidean metric $d(p,q) = \|p - q\|$.

title: Euclidean Distance Function
content: Defines the Euclidean distance dist(p, q) = ‖p − q‖ on points of the plane, modeled as EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2). This is the base metric underlying every distance condition in the problem.
mathContext: Points are elements of $\mathbb{R}^2$ realized as `EuclideanSpace \mathbb{R} (Fin 2)`, and $d(p,q) = \|p - q\| = \sqrt{(p_1-q_1)^2 + (p_2-q_2)^2}$ is induced by the standard inner product.

title: Metric Properties of Distance
content: The basic lemmas establishing that dist is a genuine metric: symmetry, nonnegativity, vanishing on the diagonal, positivity off the diagonal, and the triangle inequality. These follow directly from the norm structure of EuclideanSpace.
mathContext: The five lemmas verify $d(p,q) = d(q,p)$, $d(p,q) \geq 0$, $d(p,p) = 0$, $p \neq q \Rightarrow d(p,q) > 0$, and $d(p,r) \leq d(p,q) + d(q,r)$. Each reduces to a corresponding property of $\|\cdot\|$ ($\|{-}x\| = \|x\|$, $\|x\| \geq 0$, $\|x\| = 0 \iff x = 0$, subadditivity).

title: Minimum Diameter Extremal Function
content: Defines minDiameterRestrictedSets(n) as the infimum of diam(S) over all n-point sets S with integer pairwise distances. This is the extremal function f(n) whose growth rate Erdős Problem #100 asks about.
mathContext: $f(n) = \inf\{\,\mathrm{diam}(S) : |S| = n,\ S \text{ has integer distances}\,\}$. The conjecture is $f(n) \gg n$; the best known lower bound is $f(n) \gg n/\log n$ (Guth-Katz) and Piepmeyer gives $f(9) < 5$.

title: Integer Distances
content: All distances between distinct points are positive integers (equivalently, any two distinct distances differ by at least 1). This is the key arithmetic constraint.
mathContext: The condition $d(p,q) \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ for all $p \neq q$ is extremely restrictive. Integer-distance sets in $\mathbb{R}^2$ have been studied since antiquity. An old result of Erdős and Anning (1945) shows that an **infinite** set of points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with all mutual distances integers must be collinear.

title: Pairwise Distance Set
content: Defines pairwiseDistances(S) as the finite set of all positive distances realized between distinct points of S (the image of the off-diagonal under dist, filtered to be positive). Its cardinality is the number of distinct distances.
mathContext: $\mathrm{pairwiseDistances}(S) = \{\, d(p,q) : (p,q) \in S \times S,\ p \neq q,\ d(p,q) > 0 \,\}$ as a `Finset \mathbb{R}`. For restricted distance sets this set lies inside $\{1, 2, \ldots, \lfloor \mathrm{diam}(S) \rfloor\}$, so $|\mathrm{pairwiseDistances}(S)| \leq \mathrm{diam}(S)$.

title: Diameter
content: Maximum pairwise distance in a finite point set. The central quantity in Erdős Problem #100: must the diameter grow linearly with the number of points?
mathContext: The diameter $\text{diam}(A) = \max_{p,q \in A} d(p,q)$ measures the spread of the point configuration. For restricted distance sets, $\text{diam}(A) \geq |\{d(p,q) : p \neq q\}|$ since all distances are distinct positive integers. The conjecture asserts $\text{diam}(A) \gg n$ where $n = |A|$.

title: Main Conjecture
content: For restricted distance sets, diameter ≥ c·n for some absolute constant c > 0. This is the central open conjecture: the diameter must grow at least linearly with the number of points.
mathContext: The conjecture states $\exists c > 0$ such that for all $n$-point restricted distance sets $A \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, $\text{diam}(A) \geq c \cdot n$. The best known lower bound is $\text{diam}(A) \gg n / \log n$ (via Guth-Katz), while Piepmeyer's construction shows $c \leq 5/9 \approx 0.556$.

title: Strong Conjecture
content: Diameter ≥ n-1 for sufficiently large n. This stronger version claims the optimal constant is essentially 1, meaning diameter grows as fast as possible.
mathContext: The strong conjecture asserts $\text{diam}(A) \geq n-1$ for $n$ sufficiently large. If true, this would be tight: $n$ collinear points at positions $0, 1, 2, \ldots, n-1$ have diameter $n-1$ and satisfy the restricted distance condition. Piepmeyer's 9-point construction with diameter $< 5 < 9-1 = 8$ shows this fails for small $n$.

title: Kanold's Bound
content: diameter ≥ n^(3/4) for restricted distance sets. This was the first non-trivial lower bound, using combinatorial counting arguments on the distance set.
mathContext: Kanold proved $\text{diam}(A) \geq n^{3/4}$ by analyzing how distances distribute among integer values. The argument uses the pigeonhole principle: with $\binom{n}{2}$ pairs and at most $\text{diam}(A)$ distinct distances, some distance value is repeated $\geq \binom{n}{2}/\text{diam}(A)$ times, then geometric constraints on distance-$k$ graphs yield the bound.

title: Guth-Katz Bound
content: diameter ≥ c·n/log n via the distinct distances theorem. This is the current best lower bound, following from the landmark Guth-Katz result on Erdős's distinct distances problem (#89).
mathContext: Guth and Katz (2015) proved that $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determine $\geq c \cdot n/\log n$ distinct distances. For restricted distance sets, all distances are positive integers bounded by the diameter, so $\text{diam}(A) \geq \Delta(A) \geq c \cdot n / \log n$. Their proof uses the **polynomial partitioning** method and the **Elekes-Sharir framework**, reducing to counting line intersections in $\mathbb{R}^3$.

title: Piepmeyer's Construction
content: An explicit construction of 9 points with restricted distances and diameter < 5. This is the best known upper bound on the optimal constant, showing the diameter-to-n ratio can be below 5/9.
mathContext: Piepmeyer constructed 9 points $\{p_1, \ldots, p_9\} \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with all pairwise distances positive integers and $\max d(p_i, p_j) < 5$. Since $n = 9$ and $\text{diam} < 5$, the ratio $\text{diam}/n < 5/9 \approx 0.556$. This disproves the strong conjecture for $n = 9$ and shows that the linear constant $c$ (if it exists) satisfies $c < 5/9$.

title: Piepmeyer Ratio
content: Diameter/n can be less than 5/9 ≈ 0.56. This theorem extracts the quantitative consequence of Piepmeyer's construction for the linear conjecture.
mathContext: The ratio $\text{diam}(A)/|A| < 5/9$ from Piepmeyer's 9-point example provides an upper bound on the optimal constant in the linear conjecture. If $\text{diam}(A) \geq c \cdot n$ for all restricted distance sets, then $c \leq 5/9$. The exact optimal constant remains unknown.

title: Distinct Distances
content: Count of distinct pairwise distances in a point set. This connects directly to Erdős #89 (the distinct distances problem).
mathContext: For a finite set $A \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, define $\Delta(A) = |\{d(p,q) : p, q \in A, p \neq q\}|$. Erdős (1946) conjectured $\Delta(A) \gg n / \sqrt{\log n}$; Guth-Katz (2015) proved $\Delta(A) \gg n / \log n$. For restricted distance sets, $\Delta(A) \leq \text{diam}(A)$ since all distances are positive integers.

title: Distinct ≤ Diameter
content: For integer distances, the number of distinct distance values is at most the diameter. This is the key bridge connecting the distinct distances problem to the diameter conjecture.
mathContext: If all distances are positive integers, then $\Delta(A) \subseteq \{1, 2, \ldots, \lfloor\text{diam}(A)\rfloor\}$, so $|\Delta(A)| \leq \text{diam}(A)$. Combined with Guth-Katz ($\Delta(A) \gg n/\log n$), this yields $\text{diam}(A) \gg n/\log n$. This elegant reduction is the key insight linking the two Erdős problems.

title: Collinearity and the Erdős–Anning Theorem
content: Defines collinearity of a point set (all points on a single affine line). This sets up the Erdős–Anning theorem: any infinite planar set with all pairwise distances integers must be collinear, which is why the problem restricts to finite sets.
mathContext: A set $S$ is collinear if there exist $a \neq b$ with every $p \in S$ of the form $p = a + t(b-a)$. Erdős–Anning (1945): an infinite $S \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with all mutual distances in $\mathbb{Z}$ is necessarily collinear, so non-degenerate integer-distance configurations are finite.
